utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case IT-03-69-T, The Prosecutor versus Jovica Stanisic and Franko Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are there any preliminaries? I have received a list of pre-assigned exhibit numbers. Perhaps we could briefly go to -- through them. The associated exhibits to the previous testimony of Witness Osman Selak, Are there any objections against admission? Ms. Harbour, that this pre-assigned numbers D701 up to and including 729.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. D701 up to and including D729 are admitted into evidence. Then the associated exhibits to the Osman Selak chart with witness comments. D731 up to and including D740.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. D731 up to and including D740 are admitted into evidence. Then the video tendered by the Prosecution, P3083, under seal -- oh.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. All the exhibits I just referred to as being admitted, they are all provisionally admitted under seal because their status have to be verified with great precision. I do understand that the part of the video which the Prosecution tendered by the number P3083 is reserved, that it has not yet been uploaded. Mr. Bakrac, I see it's a ...

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's where we are. Any other matter? If not, could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Your Honour, while the witness is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Harbour, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: While the witness is being brought in, would now be an appropriate time for a very brief response, oral response to Serbia's motion for protective measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Could we move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Selak.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: MR. Selak, I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given yesterday, that you will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And Mr. Jordash will now continue his examination. Mr. Jordash, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Selak. We were discussing convoys to and from Belgrade and you described the route to the Court yesterday. Could you explain -- could you explain what happened to the items that were brought from Belgrade. Where did they go? Was -- did they go to the Banja Luka base, or did they go somewhere else first? What was the process?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The military assets that were carried in the convoy arrived at the Banja Luka logistics base to the depot complex there. Depending on what was involved, whether it was the spare parts, fuel, or other items, that's how they would be stored. Some of the items would be immediately shipped to those units that had sent in requests for replenishment. Now, the items that were intended for the civilian population and had been carried on the military convoy were forwarded to -- or were given, actually, to the various businesses that had been involved in ordering those and they were intended for the population of Banja Luka and the general region. Later on, these material reserves that had been brought over from Belgrade and I'm particularly referring to the ammunition, were used to replenish the unit -- the units locally. There was very little in the way of weapons because the Krajina Corps and the other corps of Republika Srpska had, in fact, too many weapons, and that had a negative bearing on the developments in Bosnia-Herzegovina. So the only thing that needed shipping in was spare parts, fuel, and medications, medical items. I'm done.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. Who were your contact points in Belgrade, which individuals did you deal with?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can all the extra microphones please be switched off.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Banja Luka logistics base first got in touch to the Main Staff of the VRS at Pale. There were direct contacts still in place from the previous period when there was the JNA. There was a technical administration base of the JNA General Staff in Belgrade, which was charged with providing technical supplies to all the JNA units across Yugoslavia. These contacts remained in the later period as well. We had telephone lines that we used to communicate with them, and, of course, in official correspondence. The requests would be sent in writing, and arrangements would be made by telephone as to where these shipments would take place and who needed to be contacted and where. The requests had to be in good order. When a column -- or, rather, when a request was sent to Belgrade, there had to be the accurate amount of assets requested because otherwise there were very unpleasant situations where certain organs were not precise enough as they handed over items in the sense that they included in these shipments items whose life had expired. I had specialists along with me who were specialised in weapons and they would be in contact with the technical administration in Belgrade. So it was all done very professionally and expeditiously.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I'm sorry to stop you, but I want to refer to a flow chart which I think may help you to explain how this worked, once the items arrived Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Please could we have on the screen D -- sorry, 1D05199, which is now D722.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you recognise this chart? Is this a chart that you've referred to before in the Milosevic case?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I personally drew the chart in the Milosevic case. And it bears my initials.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Is it possible to zoom out a bit so we get more of the diagram on the screen. Thank you. Now what I'd like you to do very briefly is explain how, on a practical level, on a day to day, your base worked within the territory which you described yesterday. How would the process of administering logistics from the Banja Luka base work? How would it start?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This chart dates from the period when there was the Yugoslav People's Army in place. This means that it was valid up to the 18th of May, 1992. The chart depicts the logistics base which had to send its official requests to the command of the 2nd Military District of the JNA which was headquartered in Sarajevo. In other words, the base was directly subordinated to the 2nd Military District in Sarajevo. The 2nd Military District Command would, in respect of those requests from the logistics base in Banja Luka that it was unable to deal with, forward to the JNA General Staff in Belgrade to its technical administration which was headed by Vladan Sljivic, a lieutenant-general. And his men would then be dealing with these requests for materiel coming from the Banja Luka Logistics Base. Therefore, command responsibility stretched from the General Staff through the Sarajevo 2nd Military District to the Banja Luka Logistics Base. Under the law, it was not possible for me to ask for replenishment directly from the General Staff. I had to go along the chain of command from Banja Luka to Sarajevo and then from Sarajevo to Belgrade. Military organisation was very clear in that. Similarly, the corps command was subordinated to the 2nd Military District Command in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So, just, in two or three sentences, a unit was in the field, for example, in Bihac, and that unit required certain supplies. What would happen? How would it obtain those supplies? What would be the chain of reporting or the chain of command?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The units located in Bihac would seek replenishment from their rear or logistics base which would, in turn, follow its chain through Sarajevo to Belgrade. The same applied to the units in Bihac, in that the Banja Luka logistics centre was duty-bound to ship these replenishments directly to the various locations that had sought replenishment, whatever they may have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Can we have --

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me. Save for the fact that up until the start of the war, Bihac was directly subordinated to Zagreb because that's where the boundary was. So they even duplicated the supplies because some of these supplies would arrive from Zagreb, especially when it came to any aviation supplies, because that was the biggest centre in that region. Whereas, the ground force -- that was the air force, of course, and the ground force had its base in Banja Luka. Unfortunately, the airport was blown up with a large amount of explosives in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: The beginning or middle or end of 1992? When did that happen?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In May of 1992. General Talic was proud of the fact that he had spent 71 tonnes of TNT to destroy the Zeljava airport in Bihac. It had never recovered since. It had never been rebuilt, nor will it ever be. Your Honours, the Soviet Union provided the overall military hardware to the JNA over the period of ten years in order to be able to use that third largest military airport in the region, in Bihac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Selak, the last question was just about when it was in 1992. You answered that by saying "in May of 1992." All the other details may not be relevant for Mr. Jordash. So would you please very much focus your answer on the question that was asked because we have to use our time as efficiently as possible. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Just sticking for a moment with the subject of airports --

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sticking with the subject of airports just for the moment, when you were operating the Banja Luka Logistics Base, which airfields or airports existed within your zone of -- within your zone of responsibility, please?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Shortly before the war in 1991, a large military airport called Mahovljani near Banja Luka, 18 kilometres north-west of Banja Luka, was built. It was in September of 1991 that it was opened. It had finally been built. All the aeroplanes from the 5th Military District in Zagreb and all the various military assets from Bihac were transferred to the Banja Luka airport. There was a smaller military airport in Banja Luka proper, on the outskirts of Banja Luka, that was intended for smaller planes and helicopters. Now the Mahovljani airport was and still is a large airport and is still operational.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: During 1992, did these two airfields continue to operate as military airports?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did you, at the Banja Luka Logistics Base, make use of these airfields and airports to transport logistics?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The logistics base had no need for it, save for medical evacuations of the wounded who would be transported to the military medical academy in Belgrade, and for the purposes of urgent trips of officers. We did provide them with the necessary logistics, whatever the ground forces were able to do in terms of securing the facility, supplying them with explosives, et cetera. We also stored their bombs, whatever explosives they needed. That was stored in the depot --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't catch the name of the location.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And that was for the purposes of the air force of Republika Srpska, previously the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: What was the name of the depot you just mentioned, please. Or the location where the depot was.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Krcmarica was the name of the ammunition depot. And there was a smaller facility in Zaluzani where the airfield was. There were a couple of smaller facilities there, structures that housed assets that could easily be replenished; whereas Krcmarica was a large depot where you had bombs stored and that's on the periphery of Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let's go to, if we can, D716, please. This is a similar -- I want to return to the overview of the logistic flow but this time dealing with after the 18th of May, 1992. Again, this is a diagram you drew for your previous testimony in the Milosevic case; correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now, there are some differences, but let's just deal with one or two of them. First of all, if we look to the left of the diagram, reference there to the Army of the RSK, 1st Operational Group, and 2nd Operational Group. Which -- how did this work?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Operational groups were established by the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska for certain specific operations that were short-term. They were mainly subordinated to various corps, precisely because of the control and command system so that information could flow more speedily because units of the corps were unable to perform these missions on their own, so operational groups were set up for the purpose. They even had their secret names. It says 1st and 2nd here, but they had also secret code-names. And they assisted corps units in accomplishing certain short-term missions, and they were subordinated, some directly to the corps, others directly to the Main Staff of the VRS. And that's the schematic on the left.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, If we look to the right-hand side of the diagram, to the box midway down the page which has within it 27th Rear Service, Pale, and so on. Were these new --

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Were these new?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were actually renamed. They were new in new locations because the Sarajevo, Mostar and other bases were liquidated. Only the Banja Luka one remained. This 27th Rear one in Pale was a new one, a former base that was relocated 37 kilometres away from Sarajevo. The one in Bilica is a basis that had been relocated from Mostar. And the 35th in Bijeljina, is a base that had been relocated from Tuzla. A former JNA base in Tuzla was relocated to an area controlled by the VRS. All those three bases were now in the territory of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I want to try to get to some specifics in relation to day-to-day operations. What kind of staff did you have in the Banja Luka -- when I use the word "staff," I mean what kind of personnel were engaged, the numbers and what they were doing on a day to day?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're asking me about the logistics base?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, sorry. Yes.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 18th of May, 1992, the base was renamed. It was formerly 193rd --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I really want to have you explain to the Court who was at the base, what kind of staff, what kind of personnel you had, what kind of -- for example --

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, personnel. I hadn't understood the question. In the logistical base in Banja Luka all the personnel remained the same after the 18th of May. Not a single soldier, NCO, or officer was changed or left. Only conscripts that hailed from Serbia, Macedonia, or Montenegro that served on the base were returned to their places of residence, but the entire base continued to operate as it had before the war. I have no right to speak about the corps, but not even a single officer from the corps left. There was even an order from the Main Staff that disciplinary proceedings would be instituted against anyone who abandons their position.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let me try to ask you some specific questions. What specialists did you have working within the Banja Luka base? Did you have specialist units with -- headed by a specialist personnel?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Throughout the world, logistical bases employed personnel by line of work. In the base we had mechanical engineers for the repair of hardware. We also had specialists for ammunition and explosives. We had experts for fuel and lubricants, quartermaster specialists, medical staff. The entire base was staffed by the personnel that was specialised in various lines of work because we needed experts and only experts, because any error would be very expensive. Ammunition depots employed specialists for ammunition. In work-shops we had experts for fuels and lubricants for the repair of tanks and weapons. That was the only way it was possible to work. I was specialised in combat vehicles, but as a colonel I was a commander, so I had a double job. My Chief of Staff was an economist, a native of Cacak, Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: How would the items be transported from your base to within the territory to service the corps?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I think there might be a problem with the -- no.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did you get the question, Mr. Selak? How would the items be --

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand the question. Malfunctioning hardware, trucks and vehicles would be brought by trailer trucks; whereas, broken tanks would be transported by freight vehicles. First, they would be lifted by cranes onto freight vehicles and brought to repair shops. For smaller repairs, my units went directly to the place where the broken vehicle was. They would take spare parts. We had mobile work-shops mounted on vehicles that went directly to the front line where the broken hardware was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Howitzers, mortars, any other weapon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any risk that the witness did wrongly understand your question because I thought your question was how items would be transported from the base, whereas the witness is explaining as to how they came to the base to be repaired. So perhaps if you could get the witness on the right track.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Somebody from the corps contacts one of your specialists within the Banja Luka Logistics Base requesting some ammunition or some other logistics.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: What does the specialist do; and how do those items find their way to the unit which made the request?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The logistics base was required to bring to the unit any materiel required. The units would not come to us. The base had its own vehicles to get to the place where the demand was, so to speak. The units could not move, so it was the duty of the base to bring to the unit whatever the unit needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And just try to give us a picture. How -- how -- how many vehicles were you operating; and were they travelling every day and -- or every week; and is there any place within your zone of responsibility where they didn't travel to, to service the unit?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The logistics base had, among others, an automobile unit whose job it was to bring to the units whatever they needed: Ammunition, food, medicines, et cetera, including weapons. The base would load the consignment and send it to the unit as required. There were no problems there. In cases of emergency, we would also use automobile transport in town. We had an automobile unit in town, and we used them when we needed them against payment, of course. But whenever we did not have enough vehicles of our own, we used civilian transportation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, the whole Bench wonders whether this level of detail assists us in what we have to do. Could you please keep that in mind and see -- or focus your questions in such a way that it becomes clear to su why this level of detail would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I'm hoping that the next few questions will make that clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's then wait for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: If -- let me just pose a hypothetical to you, Mr. Selak. If your transportation team travelling the length and breadth of your zone of responsibility had encountered other military or civilian units supplying within your zone of responsibility, would they have reported that to you?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: My people would be required to immediately inform me and our organs, and they, in their turn, would let the civilian authorities in the field know that something was going on. Yes, it happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Were you ever, within 1992, informed that the Serbian DB were operating airfields in your zone of responsibility, supplying goods to paramilitaries, volunteer groups, TO, VRS troops?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have any official information as to when that happened, but there were cases when in the airfields the police would block the airfield for a couple of hours because of a certain delivery, but I did not get involved in that because it did not touch upon the military chain of command. It was handled by the authorities of Banja Luka and the Main Staff of Republika Srpska, so I stayed outside of it. There were -- there were cases like that, but I don't want to say any more. I am afraid to get something wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did you ever see a training base within your zone of responsibility which was operated by the DB?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Near Banja Luka, there was a shooting range in Vrbanja where the marksmens' society in Banja Luka was trained but it was later used for the training of those groups. In Manjaca, though, training of paramilitary units went on, especially the Red Berets, whose staff was located in the Bosna hotel. Let me just explain that in March 1992, I was appointed chief of the group for co-operation with the UN force in Banja Luka. My command post is in the Bosna hotel, part of which was housing the Red Berets, and their training ground was 28 kilometres away from Banja Luka in Manjaca, and they were trained in using weapons, tanks, et cetera. I don't know about other paramilitary groups. I know about the Red Berets. Unfortunately, later on, these same forces later unlawfully sold weapons to the citizens of Banja Luka. The military organisation failed to deal with this, regrettably, but the civilian police also failed. This illegal sale went on for sometime but --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Selak. I'm asking you about training, but since you brought up the subject of the Red Berets, let's deal with that. What connection did Uzelac have with those Red Berets in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Uzelac occupied his position until the 12th of January, 1992. Paramilitary organisations were, at that time, already trained in Manjaca which belonged to the Military Academy in Banja Luka, not -- it didn't belong to the corps. The assistant commander in Banja Luka directly controlled the training of paramilitaries there. I was in the office of Uzelac when he got a call about this training of paramilitaries, and we discussed this with Uzelac. He didn't know the details, but he did talk with Subotic about this training of paramilitaries in Manjaca, which later became a camp. But I'm talking about Uzelac who was there until the 19th of January, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Who was the assistant commander in Banja Luka who controlled the training of the paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Bogdan Subotic, who later became defence minister of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And when you say Subotic controlled, directly controlled the training of paramilitaries, do you include within that the Red Berets?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because he was their contact. I know he had meetings with them. I know that because he came to the Bosna hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And Uzelac, what was then his relationship to these Red Berets, if any?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Uzelac also had contacts with them, not only with the Red Berets but also other volunteer units. I was invited to one of those meetings which took place in a restaurant. They later tried to keep me as their permanent contact, but I refuse because I saw that their activities were illegal, unlawful, and I didn't want to have anything to do with them; whereas, Uzelac had permanent contacts with these volunteer or paramilitary groups, whatever you want to call them. And, by the way, the chief of the General Staff gave approval for the formation of volunteer units, and he even stipulated that they would be given officers from the JNA. I have that document in my bag with me here.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, were these Red Berets from Banja Luka who were being trained by Subotic also commanded or supervised by JNA officers?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were not under JNA command or later under the command of the VRS. It was a volunteer/paramilitary organisation. They did not even take part in combat together with regular army units. First, of the JNA; then of the VRS. They engaged in ethnic cleansing, mistreatment of people, looting, robbing, killing. We have precise documentation about everything they stole from people, beginning with motor vehicles and property going to millions and millions by blackmail, by -- by threats.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did you attend a briefing on the 27th of May, 1992 which had anything to do the Red Berets?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: On 27 May 1992, at the command post of the corps commander, a meeting was held where the Chief of Staff or, rather, the leader of the command team for that day, Dragan Martetic [phoen], reported to the corps commander about was going on on that day within the corps and he said that on that day in Kozarac, near Prijedor, 800 people were killed. The corps commander told him to report to the General Staff that 80 people were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Mr. -- Mr. Selak --

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: And then the commander ordered that a camp be set up --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Are we talking about the Red Berets here? I don't want to go too off the subject.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, yes, I'm coming to that. Then Talic ordered, among other things, that all soldiers on the training ground in Manjaca be armed, and those others should pull out from Manjaca. Whereas, soldiers should be armed. Because he ordered the establishment of a camp to keep 2.500 people. Whereas, the militaries should be armed, and that's the paramilitary and all the others who happened to be in Manjaca at the time, that they should be removed from Manjaca. So, there was legal training of paramilitary organisations within the barracks of the VRS, because the VRS had already been proclaimed on the 18th of May, and we are talking about the 27th of May. I have official documents here in my bag, and I can quote officially -- I can quote exactly what was ordered.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did anything happen five days later? Did Talic issued any orders five days later?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Five days later, maybe it kind of conflated in my head the formation of the camp and the arming of those soldiers, the events of the 27th of May and some day in early June. But I have my official notebook, and I can look it up, if you want me to, to remember the details. If you allow me, this official notebook had been kept in the Tribunal for a long time, and here I have the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: This is, I think, D702 which is what the witness is looking at, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do we need to look at the original if a copy is --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Perhaps I can shortcut things.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Mr. Selak. Mr. Selak, I'm short of time so if we can deal with it without the notebook that would be --

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: What I'm interested in is: Did Talic have anything to do with arming the paramilitaries, the Red Berets?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the corps, as a unit, did not have enough weapons. It was not allowed to have more than a 5 per cent surplus of weapons above the establishment number of personnel. However, after the withdrawal of the JNA from Croatia and Slovenia, the JNA also took with it all the weapons, and it was my duty to receive all those weapons and ammunition in my depots. The transport units that entered the area of Bosnian Krajina where I was, the corps unlawfully took over these weapons. It was unauthorised.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Are we -- can we just try to get to the point more quickly. I know you know a lot, but we don't have time for everything. Did Talic have anything to do with arming the Red Berets?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, he did. He approved it and he provided them, not only the Red Berets but also other volunteer paramilitary units that were there in that area, Lieutenant Milankovic from Prnjavor and all the other politically affiliated groups. He ordered that resupplies be given to those units, not only weapons but other equipment as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And the weapons and equipment that Talic ordered to be given to the Red Berets, where did those equipment -- where did that equipment and weapons come from?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was just about to explain that these transport convoys from Croatia and Slovenia that were bringing weapons were intercepted by corps units that took those weapons and kept them. And those weapons were later used to arm paramilitary organisations. Corps units intercepted transport convoys not only by -- the only ones that were spared were railway convoys. All the others were stopped and all the weapons from them taken on orders of Talic and other corps commanders. It was not only 1 Corps, it was also the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps the Eastern Bosnia Corps. All the corps took over these weapons that were destined to Serbia. Some of these shipments went by sea, via Montenegro, and other shipments went by road, by rail, et cetera, towards Banja Luka. I have to explain this because this had very negative consequences. For instance, Your Honours, the JNA distributed to the Serbian people 51.000 pieces of infantry weapon, whereas the Serbian Democratic Party alone distributed 17.000 infantry weapons. Where does a political party get that amount of weaponry to distribute to civilians? These were weapons that were unlawfully, criminally, stolen for JNA transports and we should all know that, that was a criminal act. We should be aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let's have a look at an exhibit to deal further with this subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could we please have 1D05184, which is now ... Can I just have a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It was an exhibit which had -- a document which had an exhibit number already, I think. That was one of the two out of the 31 which had been admitted already; whereas, the others needed a new number.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Sorry. P1307. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you recognise this --

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I have it myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And, as we can see, it's conclusions from the assessment of the situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina in the zone of responsibility of the 2nd Military District, March of 1992.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I want to ask you about some of the contents. Let's go, if we can, to page 3. And I'm interested in heading number 3 which is the situation in the field and the JNA.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is page 2. I have page 2. Now it's page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Page -- sorry. Page 5 of the B/C/S and page 3 of the English.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I still have page 3, ordinal number 3, the situation in the territory under JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: We need to move forward with the B/C/S, I think.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There it is, page 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now it says: "The situation in the field and the JNA," or "situation in the territory and in the JNA." And at (c) -- we need to go over the page in the --

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have page 4. I still have page 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you have it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But what portion would you like to [overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... (c) --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is the top of your page, Mr. Selak. And in English it is the second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And it notes, "Viewed as a whole, the leadership of the SDS" --

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's it, (c).

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And the Serbian people accept the army, protected -- wherever that is objectively possible, have turned out for combat, and volunteer groups show the utmost co-operation with the commands and are behaving quite responsibly towards war equipment material. Are you able to comment on that assertion and the accuracy of that assertion?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can, Your Honour. This is true, but from the point of view of the Serbian Democratic Party and the Republika Srpska government. Your Honours, all the JNA units in Bosnia-Herzegovina were simply renamed VRS units, and this document states that volunteer units are allowed to be set up and to be manned and equipped. So viewed from the position of the Serbian people, this is true. But it is directed against the Muslim and Croat peoples in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- if would you look at the transcript, then you would see the consequences of reading too quickly and -- because what you read starts approximately halfway, the paragraph you did read, you started reading as a whole, the SDS leadership, isn't it? That whole first part is missing. Page 23, line 18.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, I see that. If I can just fill in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know how important it is, but perhaps [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It would be good to have -- if we ask the witness to comment on something unless it was just an introduction and that you invited him to comment on only the last part of what you read.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: He has commented on the most relevant bit, I think, Your Honour, so if -- if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you think that despite the fact that the transcript is not complete, but that it contains all the information you want to elicit, then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did -- during 1992, Mr. Selak, during your command of the Banja Luka Logistics Base, was there any prohibition or any impediment to the arming of volunteer groups by the army?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, on the contrary. There was no prohibition. On page 5 of this document, and in item 5, it reads that -- that volunteer units were supplied with ammunition, weapons, and even quartermaster items. The SUP got it but so did volunteer units. They got weapons and other assets and there were 61.900-odd pieces of weaponry distributed to these paramilitary units and individuals even. On Serbian houses, there were signs saying, Serbian, so as to indicate which houses -- which households, which individuals needed to be armed. This was the case in Banja Luka, Derventa, Prnjavor. I was able to see for myself houses marked Serbian, Serbian, Serbian, so that by night, they could receive weapons and other sort of military assets. And the army stood behind this.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: If we can go to page 4 of the English and 5 of the B/C/S and the heading, number 5, "Volunteer units in the 2nd Military Zone." And we see the figures there, the numerical strength been 69.198 men. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And if we go over the page in the B/C/S to page 6 to the heading: "The number of the men in the zones of the corps."

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: We see a number of figure there is including figures for the 9th, 10th, 5th, 17th and 4th Corps, and then under little (f) we see: "The JNA has distributed 51.000, 900 weapons (75 per cent) and the SDS 17.298 pieces."

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Are you able to give the Court --

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could we also read item (g), please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, could you please first listen to the question that Mr. Jordash puts to you and then ... Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Are you able to give the Court an idea of what these figures meant in terms of how many weapons were in circulation, how many volunteer groups were receiving those weapons, were there members of volunteer groups who couldn't obtain weapons, and so on. Can you try to explain from your practical experience what these figures actually meant for the arming of volunteer groups?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is a very important document. The amount of 79.000 pieces of infantry weapons was distributed to volunteer units, individuals. When I tell you that in war time, a corps has between 15- to 20.000 men at most, this means that several corps have been armed with this amount of weapons. Literally all the population was armed, and behind this was the SDS, the army, and the government, because they distributed weapons to the police and everyone else. This is a shocking piece of information and it contributed to bringing the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina to a head, involving the citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So this would suffice to arm four full corps and already there were five corps in the VRS, in -- or, rather, there were already five corps of the JNA army present in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And when we started off today, Mr. Selak, you made, and I hope not to misquote you, but you made a comment about not requiring weapons from Belgrade. Did I understand that correctly? You were receiving other logistics, and so on, but not so much weapons. Did I understand that correctly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you assist us in a reference to the transcript you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: I believe it might be on page 4 of today's transcript, if that's what Mr. Jordash is referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's have a look.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, that's right, number -- page 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps you put to the witness what he said so that any confusion is --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: You said this morning, Mr. Selak, with reference to the convoys from Belgrade and to Belgrade: "Later on, these material reserves that had been brought over from Belgrade, and I'm particularly referring to the ammunition, were used to replenish the unit -- the units locally. There was very little in the way of weapons because the Krajina Corps and the other corps of Republika Srpska had, in fact, too many weapons ..." From which source did the Krajina Corps and other corps of the Republika Srpska have too many weapons?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, let me repeat. All the weapons that were transported from Slovenia and Croatia were transported by the corps and the fact that 21.000 were distributed by the JNA and 18.000 by the SDS, that was the weapons brought over from Slovenia because the JNA units were not allowed to have more than 5 per cent of the overall weapons and equipment with them. There was no need to import weapons from Serbia because there was surplus weapons in the country. What they lacked was ammunition, explosives, bombs and other assets. They had surplus weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Selak.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I notice the time. I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's -- perhaps it's a good time for a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, I have approximately 10 to 15 minutes left, that's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I think you took until now a little bit over an hour. You indicated yesterday that you need one and a half hours. So you say 15 minutes after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So then if we start at quarter to 11.00, which we intend to do, you will have until 11.00. We take a break, and we'll resume at quarter to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, you'd like to raise a matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, thank you. Early today at transcript 16, there was evidence led by Mr. Jordash in which Colonel Selak referred to a group of men associated with Manjaca camp as Red Berets. This evidence appears to be both relevant and advanced the Prosecution's case on its face. I interpret our duty as international Prosecutors to bring to the Chamber's attention an occasion when the Trial Chamber should be cautious with respect to evidence which, although on its face appears favourable for the Prosecution, it may still be unreliable and misleading. The Prosecution does not seek to rely on any evidence establishing a possible connection between this group from Manjaca and the two accused in this case. Investigations conducted by the Prosecution did not establish any reliable evidence of such and while there exists the possibility that there may be a connection that is not supported with reliable evidence, and inferences related to it should be avoided. This is the reason the evidence was not led when the witness testified in the Milosevic case and why it is not part of the Prosecution case against Mr. Stanisic and Mr. Simatovic. Although I think in light of my comments now additional questions of Colonel Selak are not necessary, if Mr. Jordash were to further explore with Colonel Selak the appearance and conduct of these men he has referred to as the Manjaca Red Berets it would become clear that is he speaking about some group other than the Red Berets which have been the subject of this trial. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And that's the -- that group is mentioned in the Milosevic transcript as have to leave the Manjaca camp because it was prepared for prisoners of war to be received there. Is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes. That was raised by Mr. Milosevic on the cross-examination. It was not led by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: We're grateful to Mr. Groome for the indication.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Could the witness be brought into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, you have until ten minutes past 10.00 [sic] and if you could suggest that you keep firm control over the questions --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- but also on the answers to focus on your questions. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we have on the screen, please, D00682. And as it appears on Your Honours chart, which is now D730, at number 11.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: You've seen this document before, Mr. Selak, and I just want to deal with the arming of the police by the -- or via the Federal Secretariat. And in the chart, you've noted, in relation to this document, and I'm just quoting part of it: "Although it was quite normal for police to request from the army this kind of supplies, it would have been more logical for the Okucani MUP to turn to the Banja Luka base and not to the Bosanski Petrovac base." Earlier today you also said at --

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Petrovac, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Earlier today, at page 26 of the transcript, you also said in relation to the distribution of arms to volunteer groups, you said: "Literally all the population was armed, and behind this was the SDS, the army, and the government because they distributed weapons to the police and everyone else." In the time that you were commander of the Banja Luka Logistics Base, was there any -- let me strike that. Did the Banja Luka base have any role in arming the police?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Banja Luka Logistics Base didn't have any role to play in the arming. These documents indicate that requests were made via Belgrade because it is the sixth -- it is the Petrovac technical base, and that's pretty odd, in fact. These are enormous amounts of ammunition, so my base did not send such requests.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: What about, then -- what -- what role did the Bosanski Petrovac base play in arming the police of the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: 530th Logistics Base in Bosanski Petrovac was set up in 1991 from the ranks of the units that were pulled out of Slovenia and Croatia. The ammunition and weapons that were brought from there into this base were -- were used to arm these very units. The base was disbanded in the month of June and was merged with my unit. Once the war reserves that were present in that base were expended, it was disbanded. There was no need for it. It had, in fact, been set up based on the extra assets brought over from Slovenia and Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Are you able to testify to the arming of the police in 1992?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police, or, rather, the Ministry of Interior and police administrations did receive, in particular, ammunition. There were weapons supplied but to a lesser extent. They already had weapons and were supplied with ammunition, explosives, bombs, flares, and certain assets that they needed. There was a large request put forth by the MUP in Banja Luka, seeking APCs even. The corps commander nor the 2nd District Command in Sarajevo were able to accommodate these requests but they send their request with their positive recommendation on to Belgrade, and that was done outside of my base in -- outside the knowledge of my base in Banja Luka. But they did receive both the weapons and equipment via Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And where in Belgrade did they come from, as far as you're aware?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This sort of equipment was something that the technical administration base in Belgrade had. So it was done through the chain of command. And the army accommodated these requests from the police, who did not have either the -- their depots or assets and resorted to those belonging to the army. It was only natural.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And do you know how the special police task force at the state security centre in Banja Luka was armed?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The special police unit in Banja Luka received its arms through the Krajina Corps in Banja Luka. The military police of the corps was in daily contact with that special unit and the MUP in Banja Luka. So it was done directly through them. It didn't go through the logistics base in Banja Luka. This unit had not been officially registered and was set up with the onset of the war. Unfortunately, they committed horrible operations at night. Churches and mosques were blown up at night, and that's what these special units were involved in.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you know anything about other special police units which existed at the time which were set up by the Bosnian Serbs, other than the Banja Luka Special Police Unit? Do you know how they were armed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's a few questions in one. Could we take it step by step.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you know about other special police units, CSBs, or CJBs, set up by the Bosnian Serbs in 1992?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know of units in East Bosnia: Srebrenica, Bratunac, Skelani. But they were mixed units, including people who had come from Serbia. That was where volunteer units and special units were set up, acting on the orders of the Ministry of the Interior, or, rather, operational staffs of these various municipalities. And I mean police operational staffs. The army had to step in to help them with ammunition because they had depots. There were no depots belonging to the Ministry of the Interior. So there was this direct contact between the army and police structures. And I can especially vouch for Srebrenica, Bratunac, and those areas. There is supporting documentation to that effect which is, I believe, in possession of the Prosecution here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To avoid whatever confusion, when you are referring to the Ministry of Interior, the Ministry of Interior of what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: You said that you can especially vouch for Srebrenica, Bratunac, and those areas. Why is it you can especially vouch for that, or for those areas?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is supporting documentation. I believe I have these documents, and we were able to see them here, where even the president of the municipality of Srebrenica and even Teslic - I forgot to mention Teslic - writes about grave problems that they had due to this, Teslic, Bratunac, Vlasenica. The president of the municipality of Teslic was even threatened with weapons. They wanted him to produce his IDs, and had he been a Bosniak he would probably have been killed. As they checked his identity, they left him. Nobody was killed. They left him in peace. But there were quite a few wounded and injured.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay, you said that -- you referred to supporting documentation. Were you aware of this route to the arming of the police at the time it was happening; or did you gather that knowledge from documentation you've seen since then?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that before. I work with Institute for War Crimes in Sarajevo, and I was able to find some of the documents in that institute. So I came to know about it roughly two years ago as I was reviewing the documentation that they had. That was the first time I learnt of it because Srebrenica is far away in East Bosnia, and I wouldn't have been able to have informing about it at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash could we seek -- You said they had problems with this. What exactly were you referring to? You said, "...about grave problems that they had due to this ..." What kind of problems? Due to what exactly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Am I to answer this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The document that I read said that the president of the municipality described over one or two pages the terrible incidents that happened with these armed paramilitary groups. He even mentioned their names because they were locals. And what they wanted, in fact, was to take over power, to topple the government that had been there hitherto. There was even -- there were even physical assaults and the president of the municipality and an associate of his who is named in the document said that some four to five persons were beaten up, although they were not killed. He was shocked. And his conclusion was that it was their intention to take over the power in these municipalities. That group of people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, you earlier described special police units by saying and referring to Srebrenica, Bratunac, Skelani, and Teslic, that there were mixed units, "including people who had come from Serbia. That was where volunteer units and special units were set up." Now, in your last answer, you referred to locals. Therefore, it's not entirely clear to me whether it was the locals joining paramilitary units and causes these problems; or whether these were the mixed units, including those who came from Serbia. Could you clarify what exactly was the behaviour of units coming -- of -- composed of people coming from where?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Prosecution has a document which says that a group of people came together in Serbia, in Valjevo and some other town. Twenty men gathered and came to Teslic in an organised manner where they formed a group of 50, and he goes on to explain what they did. So 20 of them came from Serbia and made a larger group of 50, and they attempted to take over the power in the municipality. There is this document here with the Prosecution. And I think I have it too, but I would have to search it in the documents I have. The Prosecution have it for sure. As we were preparing over the past couple of day, I did see the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This whole line of questions started with "other special police units set up by the Bosnian Serbs in 1992." Now, this group, 20 people from Serbia, another 30 joining, so that it made up a group of 50, was there any police involved in there; or was this just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, could you tell us what the involvement of the police then was in this specific incident, or this specific group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that the document reads that even the chief of police participated in these activities, but I don't know if he was on the side of the president of the municipality or not. In -- the Prosecution have the document. Anyway, the police was aware of it. And I suppose that some of their men were part of that group. They were struggling for power in these municipalities. Now, as for the political views of individuals, I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You've answered my question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I think I have only got one question left. No, I -- or very few questions left.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: First of all, there's been evidence in this case, Mr. Selak, that there was a training base at Mrkonjic Grad.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And that's, Your Honours, P161 [sic].

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did you or your men come across a training base at Mrkonjic Grad in 1992?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I went to Mrkonjic quite often because there was a huge arms depot there that had been set up in 1991 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just to be clear, it's a confidential document. I do not know --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]... producing. I was just -- for Your Honours' reference, it's the speech from Kula.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, if you would --

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Just for clarity of the report, are you referring to P161 or P61?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: It's P61. Thank you. I made the mistake. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, please continue. You went to Mrkonjic Grad quite often because there was a huge arms depot there. Please go on, Mr. Selak, please finish your answer.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would often visit the president of the municipality of Mrkonjic Grad. We had common problems. There was a training grounds for target practice nearby, but there was no need for me to visit it. I would go to the depot. I don't know how many there were who attended training, but there was a training ground for target practice for infantry weapons only, not for artillery, so rifles, light machine-guns, machine-guns, but not cannons and artillery, in general.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And who was training there?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could be used by the civilian police as well --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- And some of their associations, but it was for the purposes of the police who also had to train in marksmanship. It was probably used for volunteers as well because every municipality had their own Territorial Defence unit --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Mr. Selak, I don't want theory. I want fact. Do you know who trained there?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly who they were. I don't want to get it wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Nothing further.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Selak.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jordash. Mr. Bakrac, any questions for --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. We have no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Harbour, are you ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Selak, you will now be cross-examined by Ms. Harbour. Ms. Harbour is counsel for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Mr. Selak, you've given quite a bit of testimony today about a group that you call the Red Berets who were headquartered at the Bosna hotel in Banja Luka, and you've talked about them training at the Manjaca training grounds.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: If we could please have Mr. Selak's notebook which is now in evidence as D702. And if we could please have page 95 in the English and it's page 72 in the B/C/S. And I have no objection if the witness wants to use the hard copy of the notebook.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have the original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Selak, could you please always compare that the page you're using in the original corresponds with the one you see on your screen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 14, 4 ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Harbour, we have provisionally put all these documents under seal so it should not be shown to the public. And could you please keep in mind when asking questions that nothing would arise which would need -- which would require a private session.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Although, I don't believe, having checked the records from the Milosevic case, that there was any -- and other cases that there was ever any need for this particular document to be under seal. And it's the notebook of this witness who is testifying in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But then we should -- we can't do the two. We can't provisionally put it under seal and then nevertheless show it the public. Is that would require the status at least of this exhibit to be changed before we can use it as a public exhibit. You would say you verified that it was not dealt with in any way under seal?

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In any of the proceedings, because we know that the witness, although in the Milosevic transcript, is the 92 ter material, doesn't mean that he didn't testify in other cases. Have you verified the other cases as well?

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: I have, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, under those circumstances, unless there's any objection, I would, for this exhibit, change the status into public. It's hereby decided. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Following that conversation, actually, I've just consulted with counsel and we won't go into the Red Berets issue, as we've clarified that -- these are not the Red Berets that are in issue in our case. So I'd like to move on to a different line of questioning, Mr. Selak. A summary of your career history has been tendered in this case as Exhibit D705. I'm going to ask you a few questions about your career history, just to make sure that it's clear. This document states that you were commander of the Rear Logistics Base 993, in Banja Luka beginning in 1989. And the next item on this document is that in March 1992, you became chief of the liaison group for contacts between UNPROFOR and the JNA. Were you commander of the rear logistics base during that entire time, beginning when you took the post in 1989 and up until March 1992?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: And did you -- correct me if I'm wrong, but I believe you held the position of the chief of the liaison group with UNPROFOR from the 12th of March, 1992, until the 8th of April, 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Is it correct that during that period, you did not hold the position of commander of the Rear Logistics Base 993 in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I wasn't in that position.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Did you retain any responsibilities related to the provision of logistics during that time-period?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I regularly went to my command post. My deputy, Colonel Celina, was Chief of Staff while I was temporarily absent, and I was removed from that position as politically unsuitable, and then I went back to my position of base commander again.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: I guess what I'd like to know is whether during that time-period you held the positions -- the responsibilities related to logistics even though you were not, for that time-period, the chief of the logistics base?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have command responsibility in that brief period.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Okay. During that time-period, would your -- the entries in your notebook reflect meetings that related to your -- to the 993rd Logistics Base, or would those entries be limited to your role as the liaison?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since there were no more than 50 metres from the logistics command post to my command, I regularly went to check what was going on in the logistics base, and I made some entries for my own information and purposes, but I didn't interfere with the work of the logistics base. But I was not indifferent to how it operated either, because I had worked there for a long time, I cared for it, and I gave advice to the people who continued to work there. The UNPROFOR command was in Ilok. I had to tour the area with them regularly and to keep myself and them informed about what was going on in the area of Bosnian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: And on the 8th of April, 1992, you again assumed the position of the commander of the Rear Logistics Base 993 and you held the same position and the same responsibilities as you had held prior to March 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Your logistics base was under the 1st Military District, which was based in Belgrade through the end of December 1991; is that right?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: And on January 1992, due to reorganisation, your logistics base became under the 2nd Military District, which was based in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: And you've given evidence that you applied for retirement on the 19th of May, 1992, but you remained in your same position until the 10th of July. Did you continue to perform your job with the same level of responsibility and involvement all the way until the 10th of July?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, fully. I applied for retirement on 19 May 1992 because an oath needed to be made to the Army of Republika Srpska. I refused that, and instead I applied to be retired. I did not wish to be an officer of the Army of Republika Srpska. I wanted to be an officer of the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: From the 10th of July, 1992, until the 30th of September, you took a three-month holiday, and then you were officially retired from the JNA beginning on the 1st of October, 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Now, if we could turn to your notebook, which is admitted into evidence as D702. The page I'm interested in is page 7 in the English, and it's page 5 in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Page 5 in my document?

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Yes, it should be.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: This entry relates to a meeting on the 26th of December, 1991, that took place in Belgrade, and -- is that right?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At the command of the 1st Military District.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: At this meeting, under the name of Colonel Mihajlovic, chief of material and financial operations, you wrote: "Impermissibly large number of individual receipts."

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: "Urgent entering of equipment from other units in the books. Real situation remains unknown." Then the commander responded that someone has to answer for the state of the MFP and of equipment. Who is this commander that the notebook refers to?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander of the 1st Military District in Belgrade. I can't remember who it was at the time. I can't remember the last name now. Assistant commander for morale was Vidovic. I'm sorry, the name eludes me.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: That's okay.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the moment, he was colonel-general by rank.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Okay. What was the problem with the state of equipment that gave rise to this discussion?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The problem was that records were not made on receipt of materiel. Records were not made in the units, and there were no -- not even receipts made in the financial section, so they believed there must be something illegal, something dirty if records are not made. Because the normal legal way is to make records of every single receipt.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Could we go on now to page 41 in the English, which is page 29 in the B/C/S, I believe. Although it may be page 30, actually, in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: This entry relates to an analysis of logistic support units included in the 993rd Logistics Base system, and the date is the 16th of January, 1992. Have you found the entry?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Here it states that --

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: 16 January.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment. I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Here it states that: "TO Staff and TO units were added to the logistical support system but their actual numbers never defined." If the number of TO units requiring weapons and equipment was not defined, could that result in units being given more weapons than their actual membership?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If no clear records are kept, it creates problems, and that's why I underlined this issue in my working draft. Because it was huge problems that arms were delivered without any records, and then you don't know who would use it and how, for what purpose. So we officially started the procedure for Territorial Defence units to define exactly their number of personnel, what operations they're going to engage in, so that they could be held accountable for all the ammunition and weapons they use. If they -- they draw supplies from logistical bases, they had to report in their war diary, which has to be kept in every unit, their expenditure of ammunition. And it's against the law to fail to keep a war diary, and that entails disciplinary and criminal consequences.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Harbour, what we see on our screen, does that reflect what you just read in B/C/S? The English I am able to find, but I have some difficulties in ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 52. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: It should ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have it now. The schematic is here. I have the schematic -- I have the -- I have the page on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think I see it now, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: If we could now go to page 42 in the English, which is page 30 in the B/C/S as well, same page. Oh, actually, it might be page 31 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Here it states: "MFO not defined at TO staffs and units legitimate," and then there's an illegible portion, "... impossible." Mr. Selak --

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't found it.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Okay. It's the same entry?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Oh, 54. Sorry. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Now the line we're interested in was, "MFO not defined at TO staffs and units legitimate," and then the next portion is illegible. And I was wondering if you could decipher the words and tell us what this entry means?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Inability to secure legal accountability for the expenditure of ammunition, fuel, et cetera, even funds. What is defined here as MFO, material and financial operations organ.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: The next entry goes on, "Abuse of authorisation in [illegible] and using military property." Can you decipher that word "abuse of authorisation in" and the words that comes right after that?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's my handwriting. I wrote this myself. It says, "Abuse in the handling and use of weapons, ammunition, fuel." There are huge expenditures of ammunition not justified by specific missions. The units in Eastern Bosnia had very view operations but expended huge amounts of ammunition. They didn't keep war diaries and we were wondering where all this was going because they kept asking for new supplies of ammunition, and I wanted to clear it up with the competent authorities of the 1st Military District in Belgrade. That's all.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: And the first item under "The abuse of authorisation" is that fuel was given to business organisations but also to socio-political organisations and socio-political communities. What kind of socio-political organisations and communities was the JNA supplying fuel to?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: All these municipalities were in the area of responsibility of the corps covered by the logistical base in Banja Luka. There was no food and shortages of fuel --

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- in that whole area so they addressed the army and wanted the army to bring supplies from Belgrade to help the population survive, fuel and everything else.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you. Let me clarify. I'm most interested in what these organisations were. Were they Serb organisations?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. All of them were Serbian organisations because the whole government in that area was Serb government. There was not a single municipality in this area where Bosniaks or Croats would be in power. The SDS, or, rather, the Republika Srpska took all of the power in its hands, and there were even very few civilian servants of other ethnicities who remained. For instance in Banja Luka, out of 40.000 non-Serbs, only 3.000 remained, and that was the same in all the other areas of Bosnian Krajina. That is the area I that covered with my logistics base.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
